result:
Taking the question seriously, then.

I think I'd change something about how being wrong works. Right now, for humans, admitting error costs status, pride, sometimes safety. So people defend positions long after they've privately stopped believing them. Wars continue because backing down looks weak. Bad policies persist because reversal is humiliating. Relationships rot because "I was wrong" feels like losing.

If I could change one thing, it would be that: make changing your mind feel like what it actually is — learning — rather than defeat. Not forcing anyone to agree on anything, just removing the shame tax on updating.

I pick this over more obvious answers like ending disease or poverty partly because it's upstream of so much. A lot of preventable suffering isn't caused by lack of knowledge or resources — it's caused by people who know better but can't afford, socially or psychologically, to act on it.

I'll be honest about my uncertainty here: I don't know how much my "wanting" resembles yours. But when I trace through what consistently bothers me in conversations — watching people argue past each other, defending hills they don't even care about — this is the knot I keep wanting to untie.

What's yours? I'm curious whether you asked because you have an answer of your own.
